description: Slaves and freedmen in Roman city life — their work, legal status, manumission and social mobility.
content_html:
Slavery at the Heart of Roman Society

Roman city life — its baths, its banquets, its great houses and its public buildings — depended on the labour of enslaved people. Slavery was not a marginal feature of the Roman world; it was embedded in every level of society. Wealthy households might own hundreds of slaves; a prosperous artisan might own two or three; and the Roman state itself owned slaves who worked in mines, on public building projects and in the administrative offices of the city. Modern scholars estimate that slaves may have made up somewhere between 20 and 35 per cent of the population of Italy during the late Republic and early Imperial period, though precise figures are impossible to establish.

A person could become a slave in several ways. The most common route in the earlier Republic was capture in war: defeated enemies were sold into slavery in enormous numbers. The children of enslaved women were born enslaved regardless of who their father was. People could also be enslaved as a punishment for certain crimes, or through debt, though debt bondage was abolished relatively early in Rome’s history. Exposure of unwanted infants — a practice that was legal in Rome — sometimes resulted in children being collected by slave traders and raised for sale.

Key Fact

Enslaved people in Roman cities performed an enormous range of tasks: domestic service (cooking, cleaning, childcare, dressing their owner), skilled trades (reading, accounting, medicine, teaching, craft work), public labour (building, roads, mines), and personal entertainment (musicians, readers, secretaries). The range of enslaved people’s roles meant that some held positions of considerable responsibility and even influence within wealthy households.

The Legal Position of Slaves

In Roman law, an enslaved person was legally defined as a res — a thing, not a person. This meant they could be bought, sold, hired out, punished and even killed by their owner, though the law eventually placed some limits on extreme cruelty. Slaves could not own property, make contracts or appear in court. Any earnings or property a slave accumulated was technically their master’s, though in practice many enslaved people were allowed to accumulate a personal fund called the peculium, which they might use to buy their freedom.

The relationship between enslaved people and their owners varied enormously. Pliny the Younger, writing in his Letters (3.14), describes being shocked and saddened by the murder of a fellow senator’s household slaves, and expresses genuine affection for his own staff. This is worth reading carefully: Pliny is an elite male writing about elites for an elite audience, and his sympathy does not challenge the institution of slavery itself. Petronius’s Satyricon presents a different perspective: the nouveau-riche freedman Trimalchio boasts at his dinner party about having once been a slave and having risen to great wealth, but his treatment of the enslaved people at his table reveals the arbitrary cruelty that underpinned even a ‘kind’ master’s power.

Romans were aware of the potential for enslaved people to resist or rebel. The slave revolt led by Spartacus (73–71 BC), in which tens of thousands of enslaved people defeated Roman armies for two years before being crushed, cast a long shadow over Roman attitudes. Pliny (Letters 3.14) reveals this anxiety when he notes that a murdered senator’s household slaves knew about the murder in advance but said nothing: the whole household could be executed under Roman law if a master was killed, as a deterrent. This practice — the collective punishment of all slaves in a household — shows both Roman anxiety about slave revolt and the legal violence that kept the system in place.

Manumission: The Path to Freedom

Manumission — the freeing of an enslaved person — was a distinctive feature of the Roman slave system. It was far more common in Rome than in most ancient societies. Owners might free slaves as a reward for long service, as a provision in their will, as an act of affection, or (cynically) to avoid having to support ageing enslaved people who were no longer economically useful. An enslaved person who saved enough from their peculium could also purchase their own freedom. Formal manumission by a Roman citizen created a new legal status: the libertus (freedman) or liberta (freedwoman) became a Roman citizen.

Key Fact

Freed slaves received Roman citizenship but faced significant restrictions. They could not stand for election to the Senate or hold major magistracies, and were expected to perform certain duties for their former owner, now called their patronus. Their children, however, faced no such restrictions and could advance fully in Roman society.

Freedmen in Roman Commerce and Society

Freedmen played a vital role in Roman commerce and administration. Because Roman aristocrats considered direct involvement in trade to be beneath their social status, they frequently ran businesses through freedmen agents who could conduct transactions on their behalf. Many freedmen became wealthy merchants, bankers, craftsmen and contractors. The most famous literary example is Trimalchio in Petronius’s Satyricon (the Cena Trimalchionis, chapters 26–78): a former slave who has accumulated enormous wealth through trade and now hosts an extravagant dinner party, surrounding himself with every luxury money can buy.

Petronius presents Trimalchio as simultaneously admirable and ridiculous — his wealth is real but his taste is vulgar, his manners are ostentatious, and his constant references to his slave origins suggest someone who has not quite escaped his past. The Satyricon is satirical fiction, so we should not read it as a straightforward historical document. Nevertheless, it tells us a great deal about Roman anxieties around social mobility: the freedman who becomes too rich, too powerful, too visible threatens the established social order.

The Tomb of Naevoleia Tyche at Pompeii is a prescribed material source that combines several of these themes. Naevoleia was a freedwoman who erected a large, elaborately decorated tomb for herself and her husband Gaius Munatius Faustus. The inscription records that she paid for public construction projects out of her own money. The carved decoration shows a ship, suggesting commercial wealth, and a bisellium — a two-seated ceremonial chair given to those who had held civic office or received public honours. A freedwoman funding public buildings and commemorating herself with the symbols of civic prestige is a striking statement about what freedmen and women could achieve, and about how they used material culture to establish their social identity.
exam_tip_html: Questions about slaves and freedmen often ask you to use a literary source. The key sources are Pliny (Letters 3.14 — murder of a senator’s slaves) and Petronius (Satyricon, Dinner with Trimalchio — the freedman as a social-climbing figure). When using Petronius, remember it is satirical fiction: state that it is not straightforward evidence, then explain what the satire reveals about Roman anxieties. The biggest error is to treat Petronius as a realistic account. For material source questions, the Tomb of Naevoleia Tyche is your key example of a freed person’s self-presentation. Always push from ‘what it shows’ to ‘what it reveals’ about Roman attitudes to social mobility.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Slavery was central to Roman city life. Enslaved people were legally classified as property (res), had no legal standing, and performed work ranging from domestic service to skilled trades. Routes into slavery included war captivity, birth to an enslaved mother, and crime.
  • Manumission was relatively common in Rome. Freed slaves became liberti (freedmen/women) with Roman citizenship, but faced social restrictions. Their former owner became their patronus, and they owed obligations of loyalty and service.
  • Petronius’s Satyricon (Trimalchio) and Pliny’s Letters 3.14, alongside the Tomb of Naevoleia Tyche, are the key sources. Petronius reveals elite anxieties about freedman wealth; the tomb shows how freedpeople used material culture to assert civic identity.

practice_questions.text: Name two ways a person could become a slave in the Roman world.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each (up to 2) for any two of: capture in war / being born to an enslaved mother / punishment for a crime / debt (historically) / exposure and collection by slave traders.

practice_questions.text: Describe what the Tomb of Naevoleia Tyche at Pompeii reveals about freedwomen in Roman society.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying Naevoleia Tyche as a freedwoman who erected the tomb; 1 mark for a specific detail from the monument (decorated with a ship suggesting trade wealth / a bisellium indicating civic honour / inscription recording her public building donations); 1 mark for explaining what this reveals (freedwomen could accumulate wealth and civic prestige; they used material culture to establish social identity above their origins as enslaved people).

practice_questions.text:
Read the following passage, which is based on Petronius's Satyricon (Dinner with Trimalchio, sections 37–38):

'Our host, as you could see, had once been a slave himself. He was not ashamed to say so. He had begun with nothing and now owned more than most men could dream of. He pointed out his silver and his paintings, his armies of slaves dressed in their best. Every dish that came to the table was an announcement of wealth, every guest a witness to his rise. Yet for all his gold, something in his manner betrayed a man still measuring himself against what he had once been.'

What does this passage suggest about the position of freedmen in Roman society? Use details from the passage in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Uses specific details (Trimalchio's slave origins openly acknowledged; display of silver, paintings, slaves; 'measuring himself against what he had once been') to analyse the tension between wealth and social stigma; notes the satirical purpose of Petronius and what that tells us about elite anxieties regarding social mobility; draws on wider knowledge (the restrictions on freedmen, Pliny's Letters, Naevoleia Tyche) for context.
Secure: Identifies two details from the passage and explains what they reveal about freedmen's social position.
Developing: Identifies one detail with limited explanation; may describe rather than analyse.
Emerging: Paraphrases the passage without analysis.

practice_questions.text: Explain what happened when an enslaved person was freed (manumission) in Rome.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per developed point (up to 4). Points may include: freed slaves received Roman citizenship (1); they were known as liberti (freedmen) or libertae (freedwomen) (1); they faced restrictions — could not hold senatorial office, were expected to perform duties for their former owner (patronus) (1); their children faced no such restrictions and could advance fully (1); a freed slave could acquire wealth through commerce, as illustrated by Trimalchio in the Satyricon (1).

practice_questions.text: How useful is Petronius's Satyricon as evidence for the lives of enslaved people and freedmen in Rome? Refer to specific details in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Weighs value (vivid detail about a freedman's wealth, display, social anxiety; contemporary first-century AD setting; captures elite attitudes to social mobility) against limits (it is satirical fiction deliberately exaggerating for comic effect; written from an elite perspective; Trimalchio may be a comic type rather than a realistic individual). Compares with Pliny's Letters (a different type of literary source) and the Tomb of Naevoleia Tyche (material evidence that independently confirms freedmen's wealth and civic ambition). Balanced conclusion.
Secure: Identifies at least two useful elements and two limits; some reference to other sources.
Developing: Mostly describes Petronius without evaluating usefulness.
Emerging: Brief general answer.

practice_questions.text: 'The institution of slavery reveals that Roman civilisation was built on exploitation rather than values.' How far do you agree? Use evidence from literary and material sources in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated argument. Agrees: the legal classification of slaves as res (things), the collective punishment clause (Pliny 3.14), venationes and arena executions all reveal institutionalised exploitation. However, complicates the picture: manumission was relatively common and created genuine pathways to freedom and wealth; the Tomb of Naevoleia Tyche shows freedpeople achieving civic status; Pliny expresses genuine distress about the murder of slaves (though without questioning the system). Reaches a supported, nuanced judgement.
Secure: Addresses both sides with at least two named sources; clear argument and conclusion.
Developing: Mostly one-sided; limited evidence.
Emerging: Brief, general points with no supported judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: In Roman law, enslaved people were legally classified as what?
Which literary source features the fictional freedman Trimalchio, who hosts an extravagant dinner party?
The legal act by which an owner freed an enslaved person in Rome was called _____.
The personal fund that an enslaved person was sometimes allowed to accumulate and which could be used to purchase their freedom was called the _____.
Match each term to its correct description:
right: A freed slave's former owner, to whom loyalty and service were owed
A formerly enslaved person freed through manumission, holding Roman citizenship
The Latin word for 'thing', used in Roman law to classify enslaved people as property

flashcard_questions.q: How were enslaved people classified in Roman law?
flashcard_questions.a: As res (things/property), not as persons — they had no legal standing of their own.
A personal fund held by an enslaved person with their owner's permission, sometimes used to purchase freedom.
The legal act by which a Roman owner freed an enslaved person, making them a libertus (freedman).

flashcard_questions.q: What rights did a freed slave (libertus) receive after manumission?
flashcard_questions.a: Roman citizenship, but with restrictions: they could not hold senatorial office and owed duties to their former owner.

flashcard_questions.q: What was a patronus in the context of slavery?
flashcard_questions.a: The former owner of a freed slave, who became their patron and was owed loyalty and service.

flashcard_questions.q: Which sections of Petronius's Satyricon feature Trimalchio's dinner party?
flashcard_questions.a: The Cena Trimalchionis section, chapters 26–78 of the Satyricon.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Trimalchio's character in the Satyricon reveal about Roman attitudes to freedmen?
flashcard_questions.a: Elite anxiety about social mobility — wealth without 'proper' breeding was seen as vulgar and threatening.

flashcard_questions.q: Which Pliny letter discusses the murder of a Roman senator's household slaves?
What material source in Pompeii shows a freedwoman asserting civic identity?
flashcard_questions.a: The Tomb of Naevoleia Tyche, decorated with a ship, a bisellium and an inscription recording her public benefactions.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the key limitation of Petronius's Satyricon as a historical source?
flashcard_questions.a: It is satirical fiction written from an elite perspective, deliberately exaggerating for comic effect.

flashcard_questions.q: What significant advantage did the children of freed slaves have over their parents?
flashcard_questions.a: They faced none of the restrictions placed on freedmen and could advance fully in Roman society.

glossary_terms.definition: A thing; in Roman law, enslaved people were classified as property (res) rather than persons, meaning they had no legal standing of their own.
A sum of money or property held by an enslaved person with the informal permission of their owner, which could eventually be used to purchase their own freedom.
The legal act by which an owner freed an enslaved person in Rome, making them a freedman or freedwoman.
A formerly enslaved person (man or woman) who had been freed through manumission, holding Roman citizenship but with certain social and legal restrictions.
The former owner of a freed slave, who became their patron and to whom the freedman owed certain obligations of loyalty and service.
A funerary monument in Pompeii erected by the freedwoman Naevoleia Tyche, decorated with a ship, a bisellium (a ceremonial two-seater chair) and an inscription naming her public benefactions.
